title: The brown scapular
hookLine: a small cloth worn as a sign of belonging to Mary, from Carmelite tradition

cards: At the beach, or in a locker room, it sometimes shows up: two little squares of brown wool on a pair of strings, one resting on the chest, one on the back. It isn't jewelry. It isn't a charm.
People who wear it often tuck it under a shirt where nobody sees it. Ask what it is and you may get a short answer: it's my scapular. You met it briefly on day one thousand eight.
Today is the longer answer, and it starts with a piece of clothing much bigger than two squares of wool.

teach.h: FIRST, PART OF A RELIGIOUS HABIT.
teach.b: A scapular, in the first place, is part of a religious habit: a long strip of cloth worn over the shoulders, hanging down front and back, like an apron for both sides. The Carmelite habit has one, in brown.
Over time, people who weren't friars or nuns wanted a share in Carmel's life of prayer.

teach.h: THE HABIT, SHRUNK TO TWO PANELS.
teach.b: The small brown scapular is that share: the big garment shrunk to two little panels, so a baker or a nurse can wear it under ordinary clothes.
Carmelite tradition says Our Lady gave the scapular to an English Carmelite, Simon Stock, as a sign of her protection.
Some historians question the details of that story, and the devotion doesn't ask anyone to settle them first. What the Church does say is plainer.

teach.h: A SACRAMENTAL, NOT A LUCKY CHARM.
teach.b: The scapular is a sacramental: a sign, blessed by the Church, that points beyond itself. It doesn't work by itself, like a lucky coin.
It means something only when it's joined to a life: prayer, the sacraments, trying to live as Mary lived. Wearing it says, I belong to Mary's family, and through her, to her Son.

John's Gospel has the scene this belonging grows from. At the cross, Jesus gives his mother to the disciple he loved, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold thy mother. And from that hour, the disciple took her to his own."

teach.h: CLOTHING SAYS WHO WE BELONG TO.
teach.b: Clothing often says who you belong to: a team jersey, a uniform, a wedding ring.
The scapular is the same instinct, worn quietly, close to the heart.

how: Catholics who wish to wear the brown scapular are enrolled, usually by a priest, in a short rite of blessing; afterward they wear it under their clothes, and a worn-out scapular can be replaced.

practice: A person begins wearing the brown scapular through a short rite called enrollment, usually with a priest, who blesses it and receives the wearer into the Carmelite family, once: not a purchase, a welcome.
If you pray, bring to mind Mary at the cross and the disciple taking her home. If you don't, think of something you wear or carry that says who you belong to, and what it asks of you.
